Working document for the **Fish** grouping: 89 groups, 4,502 measurements.

Scaffolded 2026-08-04 by `scripts/generate_group_notebooks.R`. **The generator is append-only**: re-running it adds sections for new groups and never touches anything already written here, so this file is yours to edit freely.

Figures and counts are static, written at scaffold time rather than computed on render. Group ids are stable (`data/clean/group_ids.csv`), so they remain the reliable way to refer back to a group even if the numbers here go stale.

# Overview

**Overview, `mg/kg (wet)`.** `n` = 10,904 measurements in 129 groups below this sub-compartment.

- @fig-biota-biota-aquatic-mg-kg-wet: fish tissue wet weights are by far our largest sample, but vary over 8 orders of magnitude, some of which is almost certainly errors.

- @fig-biota-biota-aquatic-mg-kg-dry: 20% of samples are given as dry weights rather than wet.

:::

TODO: Why is n on right so different to n = 2,374. I should know this but I don't!

> **Both answered 2026-08-05, and the second one was a real inconsistency rather than you forgetting something.**
>
> The right-hand column is now headed **`n (n outliers)`** in the panel itself, so it no longer needs explaining from outside. The second figure is how much of that category the two outlier criteria both flagged, or `(n < 10)` where the category was too small to test.
>
> The numbers disagreed because they were **counting different things**. The heading above ("n = 2,374 measurements") is `sum(MEASURED_N)`; the margin labels were `nrow()`. A Vannmiljø row carries one measurement, but a literature row can report an aggregate of fifty, so the two diverge by whatever mix of sources a group happens to have. Nothing on the page said which was which.
>
> Fixed by making it a rule rather than a patch, per your call: **a sample size is always `sum(MEASURED_N)`, and anything counting rows says so.** The margin labels and the outlier count in the bracket are now both measurement-weighted, matching the treatment `n_double_outliers` already had (PLAN.md P1.5). The heatmap fill still counts rows, because a tile counts marks drawn rather than measurements represented, so its legend now reads **"Rows"** instead of "Count".
>
> Consequence worth expecting: a category can show `2,450` over far fewer ticks and a paler tile than that suggests. That is honest, and it is 45 rows reporting 2,450 measurements between them.

:::

**By species, `mg/kg (wet)`.** `n` = 3,965 measurements across 36 species and 6 tissues.

- @fig-species-biota-aquatic-fish-mg-kg-wet clear variation between species and tissue. livers almost always contain more copper than other tissues, which is to be expected, but there's still substantial variation between species (but note small sample sizes for many groups). also plenty of outliers. probably valid to lump all fish species together, at least as first pass, although some species have medians above (S. trutta, B. bjoerna, A. brama, S. luciperca) G. morhua reference and many below (species variation or sampling artifact)

- @fig-species-biota-aquatic-fish-mg-kg-dry: much smaller sample sizes and tighter concentration distributions. typical conversion factor for dry-to-wet conversions is 5 (although actually varies with species, tissue, season, etc.); at first pass, this is consistent with graphs below. G. morhua muscle has *very* low concentrations, likely error or artefact.

## G006 Fish / Gadus morhua / Liver / Coastal, fjord / Not reported / mg/kg (wet) {#grp-G006}

`G006` **Atlantic cod**. `n` = 2,796 measurements, from **1** source (distinct `REFERENCE_ID`). Unit: `mg/kg (wet)`.

::: callout-warning
## Flagged

Gadus morhua (Atlantic cod) livers are the single largest biota sampling group in the dataset and are heavily used as a reference bioindicator of contamination across monitoring campaigns. Concentrations are reported in mg/kg wet (n = 2,796) and mg/kg dry (n = 218), roughly distributed log-normally around a mean of around (?). Fig 1a (fix cross ref) shows a large normal distribution at (mean) with distinctive secondary normal distributions at around 1e-1 mg/kg and 1e+4 mg/kg; these are likely unit errors and we have elected to remove them.
